Latifur Rahman ------ For the Petitioner.
 Miah Abdul Gafur ------ For the opposite parties.
parties:
Abdul Majid Bepari  ------ Petitioner
Vs.
Kashern Ali Maloo  ------ Opposite Party
full_judgment:
Debesh Chandra Bhattacharya J.- This Rule arising out of an application for setting aside an auction sale of certain lands held under Order 21, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for an amount of Tk. 70.84 paisa has raised certain important questions of constitutional law of some nicety.

2. The facts leading to this application are as follows: One Budhair Sutradhar obtained a decree for an amount of Tk. 68.56 paisa against Santosh Sutradhar and 13 others and the said decree-holder having put the said decree into execution got certain lands belonging to the judgment-debtors measuring 2.20 acres sold in auction and the petitioner purchased the same for an amount of Tk. 70.84 paisa on 6-9-65. The sale was thereafter confirmed on 3-11-65, and the delivery of possession of the auction-purchased land is said to have been taken on the 16th March, 1966, The opposite party filed an application on the 9th April, 1970 under Order 21, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the aforesaid auction sale on the grounds, inter alia, that he had been in possession of the disputed land on the basis of a purchase from the judgment-debtors made long before the decree in pursuance of which the sale had taken place and that the auction sale had been brought about, by fraudulently suppressing all notices, at a shockingly low price.

3. The learned Munsif, without going into the merits of the case has set aside the sale by a brief order on the ground that the decree-holder did not obtain the requisite permission from the Board of Revenue for holding the same. What was meant by the learned Munsif is that the auction-safe in question had been vitiated for want of the permission of the Board of Revenue as contemplated in section 6(3) of the East Pakistan Disturbed Persons (Rehabilitation) Ordinance, 1964 (E.P. Ordinance No. 1 of 1964). The appeal preferred by the auction-purchaser petitioner against the said order was dismissed and the order setting aside the auction sale was confirmed. The present rule has been obtained by the petitioner against the said order.

<u>4. Mr. Latifur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner has submitted that section 6 of the East Pakistan Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 has been declared to be invalid by a Special Bench of Dacca High Court in the case of Chitta Ranjan Sutar Vs. Secretary, Judicial Department, Govt. of East Pakistan and another, reported in 17 DLR (Dacca) 451. In that case a deed of sale executed by Chitta Ranjan Sutar was refused registration on the ground of absence of permission of the Board of Revenue as required under section 4 the said Ordinance. It has been held in the said decision that as the provisions of sections 4 and 6 of the Ordinance cannot be said to have imposed reasonable restrictions within the meaning of the 13th Fundamental Right of the 1962 Constitution of Pakistan, those provisions are liable to be declared void and in that sense they are also discriminatory so far as the 15th Fundamental Right is concerned.</u>

5. The 13th and 15th Fundamental Rights of the 1962 Constitution of Pakistan are as follows:-

“13. Subject to any reasonable restrictions imposed by law in the public interest, every citizen shall have the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property;

“15. All citizens are equal before law and are entitled to equal protection of law”.

A writ was issued thereupon directing the respondents of the said case to cancel the said order of refusal and register the kabala, if otherwise in order, in accordance with the provisions of the Registration Act 1908. An appeal was taken, on behalf of the respondents against the said judgment of the Special Bench of the Supreme Court of Pakistan and an ad interim order was obtained on 13.7.65 purporting to stay the operation of the order passed by the High Court. The appeal was not, however, pursued by the respondents and was ultimately allowed to be dismissed for non-prosecution on 10-6-70.

6. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has contended that the provisions of sections 5 and 6 of the Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 having been struck down by the Dacca High Court and having been declared void, there was not any question of obtaining any permission of the Board of Revenue before holding the auction sale as required under sub-section (3) of section 6 of the Ordinance and in that view of the matter the orders passed by the Court below are not sustainable in law.

<u>7. Mr. A. Gafur, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party has submitted, firstly, that the Supreme Court of Pakistan having stayed the operation of the order of the High Court upon an appeal being preferred thereto, the judgment of the High Court ceased to be operative in law and therefore the provisions of the Ordinance were applicable with full force in respect of the auction sale which has been held.</u>

<u>8. I do not think that this contention of the learned Advocate is correct. What was purported to be stayed by the Supreme Court was the order directing the cancellation of the order of refusal of registration and also the order directing registration of the document in question. The ad interim order of the Supreme Court did not contemplate and, in my opinion, could not contemplate the staying, of operation of the declaration of law as given by the High Court in their judgment. The Supreme Court has no doubt the power to set aside the judgment of the High Court in a proper proceeding and giving a different enunciation of law but that cannot be done in an ad interim order and in my view the Supreme Court did not purport to do so in the present case.</u>

<u>9. Mr. Gafur has also contended relying upon certain observations made by the Supreme Court of Pakistan in the Case of State Vs. Dosso and another, reported in 11 D.L.R. (S.C.) page 1 that the judgment of the Dacca High Court lost its effectiveness when an appeal had been preferred to the Supreme Court and the constitutionality of Ordinance 1 of 1964 had become sub judice. The learned Advocate has drawn my attention to the following passage from the said judgment.</u>

<u>“No judgment, order or writ of a High Court can be considered to be final when either that Court has certified the case to be a fit one for appeal and proceedings for appeal have been taken or when the Supreme Court itself has granted special leave to appeal from that judgment, order or writ.”</u>

<u>10. It is to be pointed out that Special leave was granted by the Supreme Court to appeal from the judgment of the High Court in Chitta Ranjan Sutar's case. On an examination of the Dosso's case it will appear that the above quoted observations of the Supreme Court has nothing to do with our present purpose. In the said case certain writs were issued by the Lahore and Peshawar Benches of the High Court of West Pakistan and certain appeals were pending in the Supreme Court of Pakistan against those orders and writs made and issued by the High Court or West Pakistan when the Constitution of 1956 was abrogated by promulgation of Martial Law, and clause 7 of Article 2 of Laws (Continuance in Force) Order, promulgated thereafter, provided that the "pending applications and proceedings before the Supreme Court shall abate forthwith". The aforesaid view of the Supreme Court was for the purpose of determining whether the proceedings out of which the appeal arose should be deemed to be pending before the Supreme Court and should abate in pursuance of the said provisions of the Laws (Continuance in Force) Order.</u>

<u>In this connection the provisions of Article 100 of 1962 Constitution of Pakistan may be referred to which was to the following effect:</u>

<u>“Subject to Article 63, any decision of a High Court shall, to the extent that it decides a question of law or is based upon or enunciates a principle of law, be binding on all other Courts that are subordinate to it.</u>

<u>And Article 63 provided:</u>

<u>“Any decision of the Supreme Court shall to the extent that it decides a question of law or is based upon or enunciates a principle of law, be binding on all other Courts in Pakistan.”</u>

<u>11. The Constitutional mandate therefore was that when a High Court declared or enunciated a principle of law or decided a question of law it was binding on all courts subordinate to it. The Supreme Court, no doubt, could make an enunciation of different principles of law or a different decision on a point of law, in which event the said enunciation or decision would have, superseded the enunciation or decision made by the High Court. But if no such enunciation or decision was made by the Supreme Court, the decision of the High Court should have prevailed and the legal consequence which naturally followed from the said decision of the High Court could not be arrested by any order of the Supreme Court which did not lay down a different principle of law. Therefore, in my opinion, the Supreme Court of Pakistan by staying the operation of the order of the High Court prevented the administrative functionaries from giving effect to the said order, but could not under the provisions of the Constitution suspend the operation of the law declared or enunciated in the judgment of the High Court. Therefore, I do not think that this contention of the learned Advocate has got any force</u>

<u>12. Mr. Gafur has next submitted that the impugned auction sale took place on the 6th September, 1965 and on that very date, Proclamation of Emergency was made by the President of Pakistan and in view of amended provision of clauses (9) and (10) of Article 30 of the Pakistan Constitution of 1962 the fundamental rights as incorporated in Part II of the Constitution particularly rights contained in paragraphs 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 13 of the Fundamental Rights were suspended and as such the benefit of the judgment of the Dacca High Court in 17 D.L.R. page 451 was not available to the petitioner. In order to appreciate the contention of the learned Advocate it is necessary to set out clauses (9) and (10) of the Article 30 of the Constitution. It may be mentioned that clause (9) was not in the Constitution on the date the Proclamation of Emergency was made, but it was subsequently introduced by means of an amendment which was given retrospective effect from the 6th September, 1965.</u>

<u>“(9) Nothing contained in paragraphs 5, 6, 7, 8, 9 and 13 of the Fundamental Rights conferred by Chapter I of Part II of this Constitution shall, while a Proclamation of Emergency is in force, restrict the power of the State as defined in Article 5 of the Constitution to make any law or to take any executive action which it would, but for the provisions contained in the said paragraphs, be made shall, to the extent of incompetency, cease to have effect, and shall be deemed to have been repealed, at the time when the Proclamation is revoked.</u>

<u>“10. While a Proclamation of Emergency is in force, the President may, by order, declare that the right to move any Court for the enforcement of such of the fundamental rights conferred by Chapter I of Part II of this Constitution as may be specified in the Order, and any proceeding is any Court which is for the enforcement, or involves the determination of any question as to the infringement, of any of the rights so specified, shall remain suspended for the period during which the Proclamation is in force and any such order may be made in respect of the whole or any part of Pakistan."</u>

<u>13. From a perusal of the above quoted provisions it will appear that so far as clause (10) is concerned the fundamental rights were not really suspended but what could really by suspended by a declaration made by the President was the right to move any court for enforcement of the fundamental rights and what was provided in clause (9) was that the legislative or executive powers of the State could not be restricted on account of the rights mentioned thereunder.</u>

14. It seems to me that the provisions of clause (9) of the Article was applicable in respect of any prospective exercise of the legislative or executive power of the State and it had nothing to do with the legislations already made and if they had been rendered invalid because of the violation of any of the fundamental rights which were in existence at the time of the enactment, that defect was not cured under the provisions of this clause. It may be noted that the Ordinance in question which was promulgated on the 17th February, 1964 was valid up to the end of 1964 which was thereafter extended for 6 months up to the 30th June, 1965 and that it was further extended up to the 31st December, 1965.

15. As regards clause (10) it has already been observed that merely the right to move the courts for enforcement of the fundamental rights as specified in the said clause remained suspended but the fundamental rights as such were not purported to be suspended by the said provisions.

<u>16. Mr. Gafur has however, contended that the provisions of clauses (9) and (10) of Article 30 were enacted clearly for the purpose of suspending the fundamental rights and if they were suspended then, according to the decision of the Supreme Court of Pakistan, the laws which were bad because of inconsistency with or contravention of the provisions of the Constitution became operative with full force as soon as the cause of the said inconsistency or contravention was removed and the provisions of the Ordinance became effective against the parties concerned. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate has placed before me the case of The Province of East Pakistan and another Vs. Md. Mehdi Ali Khan Panni and others reported in 11 DLR (SC) 318, and relying upon the said decision has submitted that the laws which are void because of inconsistency with or contravention of the constitutional provisions as to fundamental rights remain unenforceable so long as the bar contemplated in the Constitution remains in force and that the said laws are not nullified or repealed because of the said inconsistency or contravention but remain merely dormant, and revive as soon as the Baris removed by any subsequent amendment or repeal of the Constitutional provisions.</u>

17. The provisions of clauses (1) and (2) of Article 4 of the 1956 Constitution of Pakistan, which were analogous to clauses (1) and (2) of Article 6 of 1962 Constitution will he relevant for the purpose of our present consideration and are set out below;

"(1) Any law, or any custom or usage having the force of law, insofar as it is inconsistent with the provisions of this point conferred by this Chapter, shall to the extent of such inconsistency, be void.

(2) The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights contained by this part shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void,”

18. Chief Justice Munir of Pakistan Supreme Court in delivering the judgment in Md. Mehdi Ali Khan Panni's case has taken the view that the word "void" in Article 4 of 1956 Constitution has been used in the sense that the provision of particular law which comes in conflict with a fundamental right, has to be ignored or disregarded and that the moment the fundamental right in question is taken away by an amendment of the constitution or otherwise, the law again becomes operative without its being re-enacted. The learned Chief Justice has been also of the opinion that the invalidity of a particular law because of its conflict with a fundamental right is different from the invalidity which may arise because of the legislative incompetence of the Legislature concerned if the Legislature suffers from an inherent lack of power to enact the law, that law would be void ab initio and it cannot come into life without being re-enacted,

19. It may be stated that in the Md. Mehdi Ali Khan Panni's case the constitutionality of the provisions of The East Bengal State acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 relating to acquisition of the properties belonging to religious institutions, like Wakfs and Debuttors, as well as the validity of certain notifications under section 3 of the said Act purporting to acquire the properties of some religious institutions of the said nature were in question, The contention was raised that the provisions of the Act and notifications in question were violative of the fundamental right as to freedom of religion as incorporated in 1956 Constitution of Pakistan. The enactment concerned was made before the Pakistan Constitution of 1956 came into force, but the impugned notifications were issued after the constitution had become operative. The view of the learned Chief Justice has been expressed in the said case in the following matter.

"There is thus a fundamental difference between a law that is made by an incompetent Legislature and a law made by a competent Legislature, but which is in conflict with a fundamental right, the former being void on general principles, that latter being void only to the extent of the repugnancy in the sense that it cannot be applied to a particular case. The former remains void unless re-enacted by a competent Legislature, the latter requires no re-enactment and, as pointed out in the Australian cases cited above, becomes fully operative when the inconsistency of repugnancy is removed by an amendment of the Constitution or the Central Law. It cannot, therefore, be said that the laws which were in conflict with the fundamental rights were not "in force" immediately before the Proclamation of the 7th October. They were void so long as they were in conflict with the fundamental rights, but the Constitution having now been abrogated the inconsistency or the repugnancy has disappeared as it would have disappeared by an amendment of the Constitution, and they regain their full operation unaffected by any constitutional limitation or restriction except lack of power ".............................." Learned Counsel for the respondents endeavored to make the point, which does not really arise in present case, that a Post-Constitutional Law, if it contravenes a fundamental right, is void ab initio like a law enacted by an incompetent Legislature. No doubt clause (2) of Article 4 imposes a prohibition on Legislation, but such legislation, if enacted, is not void ab initio. The clause contemplates cases, where inadvertently not deliberately, because no Legislature would intentionally disobey a Constitutional prohibition, the Legislature enacts a law which collides with a fundamental right, but the result there is precisely the same as in the case of existing law under clause (1) of the Article-the law is void only "to the extent of such contravention" and not void ab initio like legislation which suffers from the incident of an inherent lack of power.”

20. The learned Chief Justice appears to have been greatly influenced by the judicial views of certain foreign jurisdictions as to invalidity of a State Law coming in conflict with a Federal or Common Wealth Law, when both the State and Federal Legislatures have concurrent competence to make any distinction between the laws before the Constitution came into operation and the laws which were enacted in the face of the Constitutional prohibition regarding contravention of a fundamental right.

21. This view of Chief Justice Muir has generally been consistently followed by the Pakistan Supreme Court, excepting a discordant note expressed by Mr. Justice Hamoodur Rahman (as he then was) in the case of Abul A'la Moudoodi and another Vs. The Govt. of West Pakistan and others. 17 D.L.R. (SC) 209. The following portion from the judgment of Mr. Justice Hamoodur Rahman may be usefully quoted in order to pin-point the difference in approach between the two views:

“In the case of a law made after the declaration of fundamental rights the Constitution has placed a complete bar on the power of the Legislature to make any law which takes away or abridges any right conferred by the Constitution itself. Such law, if made in contravention of clause (2) of Article 6, is to be void ab initio but in the case of an existing law, clause (1) of the said Article, it appears, makes a distinction. It avoids it only to the extent of the inconsistency.”

It may be noticed that the other Judges constituting the Bench which decided the said case did not express any opinion in this regard as the question of the constitutionality of any Post-Constitutional Law did not directly arise in that case. But the Supreme Court Bench of which Mr. Justice Hamoodur Rahman was a member deciding the case of Chowdhury Tanvir Ahmed Siddique Vs. The Province of East Pakistan 20 D.L.R. (S.C.) 144 refused to review the law as pronounced in the judgment given in Md. Mehdi Ali Khan Panni's case although the validity of certain post-constitutional notifications affecting the fundamental right under Article 18 of the then Constitution was in question in the said case in the same way as in Md. Mehdi Ali Khan Panni's case. It should be mentioned that both in Mehdi Ali Khan Panni's case as well as in Tanvir Ahmed Siddiky's case, the constitutionality of a pre-constitution Act, viz. The East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 was mainly considered but somehow the question of the validity of the Post-Constitutional notifications under section 3 of the said Act did not receive much consideration in the judgments of the aforesaid two cases. The word 'law' as used in Article 4 of the Pakistan Constitution of 1956 appears to be wide enough to include a notification of the kind issued under section 3 of the aforesaid Act, but the act of issuance of the said notification was not properly tested in the light of the principle of constitutionality propounded by Mr. Justice Hamoodur Rahman in Abul Ala Moudoodi's case referred to above.

<u>22. It is to be thus noticed that almost all the judges of the Supreme Court of Pakistan excepting Mr. Justice Hamoodur Rahman did not make any distinction between pre-constitution and post-constitution laws. According to the said view, both kinds of law coming in conflict with fundamental rights will normally remain suspended so long as the fundamental rights remain in force and will be restored to life as soon as the Constitutional bar is removed either by repeal or by amendment.</u>

<u>23. It may be mentioned in this connection that the judicial views as expressed in the judgments delivered by the Supreme Court of India were not at first consistent but the preponderant view which has ultimately prevailed makes a distinction between a pre-constitutional law and post-constitutional law in respect of the consequence that may follow as a result of its conflict with any of the fundamental rights guaranteed under the Constitution. The said Court has developed a doctrine which has gained currency as the doctrine of eclipse, in regard to a pre-constitutional law coming in conflict with a fundamental right. According to his doctrine, a pre-existing law coming in conflict with a fundamental right becomes eclipsed by the fundamental right and is thus rendered inoperative so long as the fundamental right remains in force but if the fundamental right is taken away by necessary enactment, the shadow is removed and the law automatically comes into life and regains full force without and fresh legislative act. But in case of a post-constitutionals law coming into a clash with a fundamental right, the law is still born and is without life from its very inception. No difference is made to its condition even if the fundamental right the contravention of which has invalidated such law is removed from the Constitution it cannot come into force without a fresh legislative act.</u>

24. It is interesting to notice that another extreme view was expressed by a Special Bench of the West Pakistan High Court in the case of Hashem alias Channu Vs. Tribunal, in P.L.D. 1959 Karachi page 286 which also deserves our consideration. Chief Justice Kayani of the West Pakistan High Court who delivered the leading judgment in the case expressed his view in the following manner:

“I think we should face a void as a void and not resort to similes derived from birth or death. A simile, to be perfect" said Dr. Johnson, "must both illustrate and ennoble the subject". The phenomenon of still-born laws serves neither end. Nor does an eclipse describe a dormant law truly. An eclipse is a very transitory phenomenon, and the effect of a Fundamental Right is far from ecliptic. It were better to say, if we judged things by births and deaths, that such laws were in a state of coma. But they are not in a state of coma; they are just void. My answer to the question before the Full Bench, therefore, is that the enactments rendered void by the Articles relating to Fundamental Rights in the late Constitution are not in force in Pakistan.”

25. It has thus become necessary to examine the rationale of the conflicting judicial views referred to above. Chief Justice Munir in the judgment mentioned above has referred to Willoughby's "The Constitutional Law of the United States" and has reproduced certain excerpts from the judgments of the Court of West Virginia in Shepperd Vs. Wheeling (30 West Virginia 479) and also of the Court of Iowa in State of Iowa Vs. O'Neil, (147 Iowa 593) as quoted by the learned author, in support of the view the learned Chief Justice has taken in that case Those excerpts do not appear to represent the view of M. Willoughby fully. The distinguished author has very lucidly dealt with the nature of an unconstitutional law in some of the passages at pages 9 and 10 of Vol. I of his book. 1929 edition, to which reference may be made.

“The doctrine that an unconstitutional law is void is often stated as a deduction from the premises that constitutional law is a superior kind of law to which statute law of inferior rank is obliged to yield. Speaking in all strictness, however, this is not the case for the unconstitutional Statute is not low at all, whatever its form or however are solemnly enacted and promulgated.

“There are not and cannot be degrees of legal validity. Any given rule of conduct or definition of right either is or is not law. When therefore we describe any particular measure as unconstitutional law and therefore void, we are, in fact, strictly speaking, guilty of contradiction of terms, for if it is unconstitutional it is not law at all; or if it is law it cannot be unconstitutional. Thus when a particular so-called law is declared unconstitutional by a competent court of last resort, the measure in question is not "annulled" but simply declared never to have been law at all, never to have been in fact, anything more than a futile attempt at legislation on the part of a legislature enacting it."

26. Mr. Willoughby has also quoted the following dictum as laid down by Mr. Justice Field in the case of Norton Vs. Shelby Co. (118 U.S. 425) at page 10:

"An unconstitutional act is not a law, it confers no right, it imposes no duties, if offers no protection, it creates no office; it is in legal contemplation, as inoperative as though it had never been passed.”

27. The learned Author while considering the effect of subsequent grant of legislative power in respect of a law made by legislature without legislative competence, made the following observation (see page 11 of his book.):

"The validity of a Statute is to be tested by the Constitutional power of a legislature at the time of its enactment by the legislature, and, if thus tested, it is beyond the legislature power, it is not rendered valid, without re-enactment, if later, by constitutional amendment, the necessary legislative power is granted" and he quoted with approval the following as laid down by the Supreme Court of the United States in the case of New Berry Vs. United States, 256 U.S. 232:

“An after-acquired power cannot ex proprio vigore, validate a Statue void when enacted.”

The learned Author has also clearly dealt with the circumstances under which an unconstitutional law does not become completely non-existent but is mainly kept in abeyance because of a Constitutional bar and it springs into life as soon as the Constitutional bar is removed:

“However, it has been held that where an act is within the general legislative power of the enacting body, but rendered unconstitutional by reasons of some adventitious circumstances, as, for example, when a State legislature is prevented from regulating a matter by reason of the fact that the Federal Congress has already legislated upon that matter, or by reason of its silence is to be construed as indicating that there should be regulation, the act does not need to be re-enacted in order to be enforced, if this cause of its unconstitutionality is removed.”

It may be noticed that the view expressed by Willoughby in his commentary does hot state that any constitutional prohibition in respect of a legislation violative of a fundamental right is a mere adventitious circumstance. On the contrary, the learned author has made it abundantly clear at several places of his book that any purported legislation without the Constitutional power of legislation, to all intents and purposes, does not come into existence and is non est in the eye of law and so, is not brought into life on the removal of the Constitutional bar. The views of the Supreme Court of the United States of America as have been referred to above are more or less, in favor of the said proposition. Some of the State Courts of the United States of America appear to have laid down the law in this regard in somewhat different manner and on which some reliance was placed by the learned Chief Justice of Pakistan in Md. Mehdi Ali Khan Panni's case-but this does not appear to be an accord with more authoritative judicial and justice views. In this connection, I may refer to the following passage from Professor Cooly's "A Treatise in the constitutional Limitations" Vol 1, 1927 Edition at page 82-384, which is germane to our present discussion:

“When a Statute is adjudged to be unconstitutional it is as if it had never been. Rights cannot be built up under it; contracts which depend upon it for their consideration are void; it constitutes a protection to no one who has acted under it, and no one can be punished for having refused obedience to it before the decision was made. And what is true of an act void in toto is true also as to any part of an act which is found to be constitutional, and which consequently, is to be regarded as having never at any time possessed of any legal force.”

The following observations at page 384 of the Treatise is very significant:

“A Statute void for unconstitutionally is dead and cannot be vitalized by a subsequent amendment of the Constitution removing the Constitutional objection, but must be re-enacted.”

<u>28. It should, of course, be clearly understood that reference to the decisions under the American Constitution for the purpose of interpreting the provisions of the Constitution in another country cannot always be useful because of the fact that the Constitutions of the two countries are drafted entirely in different languages. In the Constitution of the United States there is no such provision as contained in Article 4 of the 1956 Constitution of Pakistan or Article 6 of the 1962 Constitution of Pakistan which are almost in the same terms as Article 13 of the Indian Constitution.</u>

29. The first important case of the Indian jurisdiction in which Article 13(1) of the Indian Constitution came up for interpretation was the case of Kashhavan Madhavan Menon Vs. The State of Bombay, reported in A.I.R. 1951 (S.C.) 128. In that case, the petitioner, who was the Secretary of the People's Publishing House, Bombay was charged with publishing a news sheet without any authority, as contemplated in Press (Emergency Powers) Act, 1931 and as such was alleged to be liable to be convicted under the said Act. While the aforesaid proceeding was pending against the petitioner, the Indian Constitution came into force on 26-1-50 guaranteeing certain fundamental rights and the provision of the Press Act, the infringement of which the petitioner was charged with, became void under Article 13(1) of the Constitution because of its inconsistency with fundamental right. The majority of the Judges (Kania CJ. Shastri, Mahajan, Das and Chandrasekar Aiyyar, JJ.) of the Bench has taken the view that Article 13(1) can have no retrospective operation and its effect is entirely different from the effect of the expiry of temporary Statute or repeal of a Statute by a subsequent Statute. So, according to the said view, the old law shall have to be applied to decide if the petitioner committed the offence. The minority view (Fazal Ali and Mukherjee, JJ.) has, however, held that Article 13(1) will apply to transactions which are not past and closed, and therefore the petitioner cannot be convicted under the old law.

30. In the case of Saghir Ahmed Vs. The State of Uttar Pradesh, reported in A.I.R. 1954 (S.C.) 728, a Bench of five Judges (Mahajan, CJ., Mukherjee, Das, Bose and Gholam Hasan. JJ.) of the Supreme Court of India has laid down that an amendment of the Constitution which came latter cannot be invoked to validate an earlier legislation which must be considered unconstitutional when it was passed and has quoted with approval the observation of Prof. Coolly Preferred to above in which the distinguished author has stated that a Statute void for unconstitutionality is dead and cannot be vitalized without re-enactment. The meaning and import of the word "void" as used in Article 13(1) of the Indian Constitution came up, thereafter for consideration before a Bench of three Judges in the case of Behram Khurshid Pesikaka Vs. The State of Bombay, reported in A.I.R. 1955 (S.C.) 123, and Venkataram Aiyyar, J. in delivering the leading judgment of the majority view drew a distinction between the invalidity arising out of the lack of legislative competence and that arising by reason of a check imposed upon the legislature by the provisions contained in the Chapter on Fundamental Rights. The learned Judge, was of the view that word "void" in Article 13(1) of the Indian Constitution should be construed as meaning, in the language of the American Jurists, as "relatively void" and that if it was a check imposed upon the legislative powers of the Legislature the further question was to be enquired was whether it was for the benefit of an individual or of the general public. If it was, according to the learned Judge, for individual benefit, it could be waived and violation thereof, in such cases, did not make the law "absolutely void" but "relatively void". It was held by the majority in that case that the right guaranteed under Article 19(1)(f) of the Indian Constitution was for the benefit of private owners and any law violative of such a right might be enforced, if waived by the person for whose benefit it was en-grafted in the Constitution.

31. This judgment was, however, subsequently, reviewed and was ultimately referred to a Constitution Bench of five Judges, which held the majority view of the earlier Bench to be wrong. Chief Justice Mahajan in delivering the judgment of the majority of the Constitution Beach (with concurrence of Mukherjee, Vivan Bose and Ghulam Hasan, JJ.) has pointed out that there is no scope for introducing terms like "relatively void" coined by American Judges in construing a Constitution which is not drawn up in similar language, and refused to endorse the view of Venkataram Aiyyar, J. who drew a distinction between two kinds of declaration of unconstitutionality, one arising from lack of legislative power and the other from conflict with a fundamental right. The learned Chief Justice has very clearly stated that both the declarations go to the root of the legislative power itself and that there is no real distinction between the two. As regards the meaning of the word, "void" in Article 13(1), the learned Chief Justice representing the majority view has been of the opinion that the matter stands concluded by reason of the majority decision in A.I.R. 1951 (S.C.) 128 which had held, according to this judgment, that after the coming into force of the Constitution the effect of Article 13(1) on the laws repugnant to the fundamental right was to nullify them and make them ineffectual and nugatory and devoid of any legal force of binding effect, although such laws will be available for determination of the rights, arising and obligations incurred prior to the enforcement of the Constitution and for determination of the rights of the persons having no fundamental rights. As regards Article 13(2), it has been pointed out that it embodies a clear and unequivocal mandate, which indicates that there is no competency in Parliament or a State Legislature to make a law which comes in a conflict with fundamental rights after the coming into force of the Constitution.

32. Mr. Justice S.R. Das as Acting Chief Justice of Supreme Court of India, with whom Bhagwati, Venkataram Ayyar, Immam and Chandra Sekhar Ayyar. JJ. agreed, in delivering the judgment of the Bench developed the doctrine of eclipse in respect of an existing law coming in conflict with a fundamental right guaranteed under the Constitution in the case of Bhikaji Narain Dhakras Vs. State of Madhaya Pradesh, reported in A.I.R. 1955 (S.C.) page 781. The following observations of the learned Acting Chief Justice may be referred to:

"The true position is that the impugned law became, as it were eclipsed, for the time being, by the fundamental right. The effect of the Constitution (First Amendment) Act, 1951 was to remove the shadow and to make the impugned Act free from all blemish or infirmity...................................................

“The American authorities refer only to Post-Constitution Laws which are inconsistent with the provisions of the Constitution. Such laws never came to life but were still-born as it were. The American authorities therefore, cannot fully apply to Post-Constitution Laws which were perfectly valid before the Constitution. But apart from this distinction between Pre-Constitution and Post-Constitution Laws on which, however, we need not rest our decision, it may be held that these American authorities can have no application to our Constitution. All laws, existing or future, which are inconsistent with the provisions of Part III of our Constitution are, by the express provisions of Art. 13, rendered void to the extent of such inconsistency. Such laws were not dead for all purposes They existed for the purposes of Pre-Constitution rights and liabilities and they remained operative, even after the Constitution, as against the non-citizen.”

33. This opinion of Acting Chief Justice Das has been interpreted by the noted Indian Jurist Mr. H.M. Seervai in his book "Constitutional Law of India", Vol. I, 1968 to mean that the learned Acting Chief Justice (as he then was) did not really make any distinction between Pre-Constitution and post-Constitution Laws and practically over-ruled the decision given in the ease of Behram Khurshid Pesikaka Vs. State of Bombay reported in A.I.R. 1955 (S.C.) 123. On a close reading of the judgment delivered by the learned Acting Chief Justice it does not appear, however, that the learned Author was quite correct in his appreciation of the said view. It may be mentioned that Mr. Justice Das delivered a separate judgment in Behram Khurshid's case A.I.R. 1955 (S.C.) 123 in expressing his disagreement with the majority view on the question of onus of proof and stating that Art. 13(1) did not in terms make the existing laws which were inconsistent with fundamental rights void ab initio for all purposes, but the learned Judge took care to distinguish his own view from that of Venkatarama Ayyar. J. relating to waiver of constitutionality, the fundamental rights being a mere check on legislative power and the effect of declaration under Article 13(1) being "relatively void".

34. In Bhikaji Narain's case, the question of voidness of a pre-constitutional law coming in conflict with a fundamental right and the effect of subsequent amendment of the Constitution, removing the constitutional bar were under consideration, and although the observation of Acting Chief Justice Das as quoted above may lend itself to be interpreted to mean that he was making no distinction between pre-constitutional and post-constitutional laws and moved very close to the view of Venkatarama Ayyar, J. in spite of his express dissent from the said view in regard to the fundamental rights being a mere check on legislative power in the case of Behram Khurshid's case, it cannot be said that the majority decision in Behram Khurshid's case was over-ruled because the reasonings given by Chief Justice Mahajan in regard to the interpretation of Art. 13(2) of the Constitution were neither countered nor considered.

35. It has, however, been made very clear in a subsequent decision in the case of Dip Chand Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh reported in A.I.R. 1959 (S.C.) 648 in which the majority decision given by Subra Rao, J. with whom Bhagwat, Sinha and Wanchoo, JJ. agreed and expressed the view of the majority as follows:

“The result of the aforesaid discussion may be summarized in the following propositions: (1) Whether the Constitution affirmatively confers powers on the legislature to make laws subject wise or negatively, prohibits it from infringing any fundamental right, they represent only two aspects of want of legislative power; (ii) The Constitution in express terms makes the power of a legislature to make laws in regard to the entries in the lists of the Seventh Schedule subject to the other provisions of the Constitution and thereby circumstances or reduces the said power by the limitation laid down in Part III of the Constitution; (iii) it follows from the premises that a law made in derogation or in excess of that power would be ab initio void wholly or to the extent of the contravention as the case may be; (iv) the doctrine of eclipse can be invoked only in the case of a law valid when made, but a shadow is cast on it supervening constitutional inconsistency or supervening existing statutory inconsistency; when the shadow is removed the impugned Act is freed from all blemish or infirmity.”

36. Chief Justice Das who was a member of the said Bench, delivered separate judgment expressing his dissenting view in the following manner:

A Post-Constitution Law may infringe either a fundamental right conferred on citizens only or a fundamental right conferred on any person, citizen, or non-citizen. In the first case the law will not stand in the way of the exercise by the citizens of that fundamental right and, therefore will not have any operation on the rights of the citizens but it will be quite effective as regards noncitizens. In such a case the fundamental right will, qua the citizens, throw a shadow on the law which will nevertheless be on the Statute Book as a valid law binding on non-citizens and if that shadow is removed by a constitutional amendment, the law will immediately be applicable even to the citizens without being re-enacted. Whether a Post-Constitution law of other kind namely which infringes a fundamental right guaranteed to all persons, irrespective of whether they are citizens or not and which, therefore can have no operation at all when it is enacted, is to be regarded as a still-born law as if it had not been enacted at all and, therefore, not subject to the doctrine of eclipse is a matter which may by open to discussion.

37. It may be pointed out that in case of Bashershar Nath Vs. Commissioner of Income-Tax, Delhi and Rajasthan and another, reported in A.I.R. 1959 (S.C) 149 the question of applicability of the doctrine of waiver in respect of a certain action taken in pursuance of a law violative of the fundamental right to equality came up for consideration Bhagawati and Subba Rao, JJ. have taken the view in the said case that it is not open to a citizen to waive his fundamental rights conferred by the Constitution while S.K. Das, J. in his dissenting view has held that when fundamental right is primarily intended for individual benefit, such a right can be waived and Chief Justice Das, Kapur, J. concurring, without committing himself in respect of other fundamental rights has expressed himself in favor of the view that the fundamental rights to equality as embodied in Article 14 of the Indian Constitution cannot be waived.

38. The Supreme Court of India after a consideration of the case laws regarding the nature of the unconstitutionally of the laws violative of fundamental rights, has laid down the law in the clearest terms in the case of Mohendra Lal Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, reported in A.I.R. 1963 (S.C.) 1019, so far as the Indian Courts are concerned, in the following manner:

“The review of these authorities therefore in our opinion clearly shows that the doctrine of eclipse will apply to Pre-Constitution laws which are governed by Art. 13(1) and would not apply to Post-Constitution laws which are governed by Art.13 (2). It is, however, urged on behalf of the respondents that on language of Art 13(1) and 13(2) there should be no difference in the matter of application of the doctrine of eclipse. It is said that Art. 13(1) prescribes that in so far as the existing laws are inconsistent with the provisions of Part III, they shall, to the extent of such inconsistency; be void. Similarly, Art. 13(2) provides that any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to, the extent of the contravention, be void. The argument is two-fold. In the first place, it is urged that the words "to the extent of the inconsistency" or "to the extent of the contravention" mean "so long as the inconsistency continues or so long as the contravention continued". We are of opinion that this is not the meaning of these words in Art.13(1) and (2). Obviously, the Constitution-Makers, when they used, the words "to the extent of" in both clauses, intended that the pre-existing laws or the post-Constitution laws should only be void as far as the inconsistency or the contravention went, i.e. if only a part of the law was inconsistent or contravened the constitutional prohibition, that part alone would be void and not the entire law. The obvious intention behind the use of the words "to the extent of" was to save such parts, of law as were not inconsistent with or in making which the State did not contravene the prohibition against infringement of fundamental rights and the distinction may conceivably introduce consideration of severability; it has in our opinion no reference to the time for which the voidness is to continue”.

39. I think the discussion on the Indian judicial views will not be complete if I do not refer to one case namely M.P.V. Sundararamier & Co. Vs. The State of Andhra Pradesh and another, as reported in A.I.R 1958 468 because Mr. H.M. Seervai has expressed the view in his commentary in Constitutional Law of India (at page 171) that the subsequent Indian decisions having taken no notice of the case have not acquired any authoritative character. Mr. Justice Venkatarama Ayyar who was responsible for importing the idea of "relatively void" as expounded in American Judicial views in the Indian Constitutional discourse in the case reported in A.I.R. 1955(S.C.) 123. which was apparently overruled by a Constitution Bench as has been referred to above, has delivered the judgment of the Bench consisting of 5 judges deciding the Sundaramier's case, and according to Mr. Seervai the subsequent Indian Supreme Court decision in the case of Mahendra Lal Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh having failed to notice the view expressed in the said case is a judgment per incuriam and as such the position remains uncertain so far as the Indian Supreme Court is concerned,

40. The following comment of the learned author may be referred to:

In Mahendra Lal Vs. State of U.P. the Supreme Court reviewed the authorities but here again Sundararamier's case was neither cited nor considered.

* * * *

It is difficult to explain the consistent overlooking by the Supreme Court of Sundararamier's case, a case which raised questions of far-reaching constitutional importance and which was argued not only by the parties to it, but in which four private corporations intervened as did the Union of India, and the States of Bihar, Madras and the U.P. It is submitted that the present position cannot be regarded as satisfactory, and it is not possible to state accurately the law laid down by the Supreme Court. For reasons already given, it is submitted that the law as laid down in Sundararamier's case is correct.

41. In order to appreciate the criticism of the learned author, it is necessary to note that one of the points in Sundararamier's case, was that section 22 of Madras General Sales Act (as applied to Andhra Pradesh) was unconstitutional as it was, when it enacted, repugnant to Art 286(2) of the Indian Constitution, which provides that "except in so far as Parliament may by law otherwise provide, no law of a State shall impose, or authorize the imposition of a tax on the sale or purchase of goods in course of inter-State trade or commerce. Venkataram Ayyar j. who delivered the majority judgment (A.K. Sarker, J. dissenting) has disposed of the above argument with the following observation:

“It would be sufficient answer to this contention that section 22 of the Madras Act is only a piece of conditional legislation, imposing tax in inter-State sales when Parliament should enact a law lifting the ban if such legislation is competent as we have held it is, then no question of unconstitutionality of the section when it was enacted could arise.”

42. Still then the learned Judge proceeds to consider the question as to the effect of constitutionality, "as the question raised has been, of late, the subject of considerable discussion in this court", and lays down the ratio decidendi in the following terms, almost in the same manner as he did in Behram Khursbid's case:

“If a law is on a field not within the domain of the Legislature, it is absolutely null and void, and subsequent cession of that field to the Legislature will not have the effect of breathing life into what is a still-born piece of legislation and a fresh legislation on the subject would be requisite. But if the law is in respect of a matter assigned to the Legislature, but its provisions disregard constitutional prohibitions, when once they are moved, the law will become effective without re-enactment.”

It may be pointed out with respect that the observations of Chief Justice Mahajan in the Bahrain Khurshid's case in refuting the conclusion reached by Venkataram Ayyar, J. as to fundamental rights being a mere check on legislative power have not been considered or referred to in this Judgment.

43. After referring to the case of Bhikaji Narayan Dhakras Vs. The State of Madhaya Pradesh, A.I.R. 1955 (S.C.) 781, which dealt with the effect of removal of a constitutional prohibition upon a pre-constitutional law rendered unenforceable because of inconsistency with a fundamental right, Venkataram Ayyar, J. expressed his opinion in the following manner.

“The result of the authorities may thus be summed up:Where an enactment is unconstitutional in part but valid as to the rest, assuming, of course, that the two portions are severable, it cannot be held to have been wiped out of the statute book as it admittedly must remain there for the purpose of enforcement of the valid portion thereof, and being on the statute book, even that portion which is unenforceable on the ground that it is unconstitutional will operate proprio vigore when the constitutional bar is removed, and there is no need for a fresh legislation to give effect thereto.”

44. The proposition of law laid down by the learned judge as above has nothing to do with a post-constitutional law becoming void because of legislative incompetency of the Legislature concerned and he was careful enough to set down limitation to the aforesaid proposition by distinguishing it from other cases in the following way:

“There is one other question to which reference must be made the decisions in Behram Khurshid Penikaka Vs. The State of Bombay and Fikaji Narayan Dhakras Vs. The State of Madhaya Pradesh both turn on the construction of Art 13 of the Constitution, which enacts that laws shall be void to the extent they are repugnant to the provisions of Part III. We are concerned in these petitions not with infringement of any of the provisions of Part III but of Art. 286(2) and, the point for our decision is as to the effect of the infringement of that provision. Art. 286(2) does not provide that a law which contravenes it is void, and when regard is had to the context of that provision it is difficult to draw the inference that is the consequence of contravention of the provision.”

45. The above quoted passage makes it abundantly clear that Sundararemier's case is no authority for the nature and character of an unconstitutional law, where unconstitutionality arises from infringement of a fundamental right, and I may say with respect that the criticism of the later decisions of the Indian Supreme Court for failure to refer to Sundararamier's case does not appear to be well-founded.

46. In this context I may also quote the view of another distinguished commentator of Indian Constitution namely, Mr. D. Basu. who was formerly a Judge of the Calcutta High Court and who in his commentary on the Indian Constitution has made the following observations at page 252 Volume I, Fifth Edition after referring to the Supreme Court cases of Bhikaji Vs. The State of Madhaya Pradesh:

“With respect, the above attempt to make a distinction between legislative competence and constitutional limitation imposed by a fundamental right had no foundation the basic principles of constitutional jurisprudence, and the doctrine of eclipse, if allowed to prevail in the wide form in which it was propounded was sure to render nugatory to a dangerous extent the incorporation of fundamental rights in the Constitution. Later decisions of the Supreme Court have however done with attempted distinction between legislative limitation and fundamental rights, and also reduced the scope of the doctrine of eclipse to a limited sphere.”

47. Thereafter, after referring to the cases of Deep Chand Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Mahendra Vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, the learned author has arrived at the following conclusion:

“It is accordingly settled that if a Post-Constitution law contravenes a fundamental right it is void ab initio and that the doctrine of eclipse cannot be applied to such law, so as to revive it by subsequent amendment of the constitution.”

<u>48. Having regard to the judicial views referred to above, I find myself in respectful agreement with the view that a post-constitutional law violative of a fundamental right guaranteed under the Constitution is dead for all purposes and cannot revive by mere repeal of the fundamental rights.</u>

<u>49. There being a positive mandate of the Constitution directing the State not to make any law repugnant to any of the fundamental rights and the Constitution itself declaring that any law made in violation of the said mandate shall be void to the extent of the repugnancy, it is clear that any subject trenching upon a fundamental right has been kept outside the legislative competence of the Legislature, and any law on such a subject in spite of the constitutional prohibition will obviously be without jurisdiction, and as such a nullity It will be a futile legislative endeavor. By incorporating certain rights as fundamental rights in one of the initial chapters of the constitutional document and directing the state not to make any law in derogation of such rights, there is a complete ouster of legislative jurisdiction of all kinds of Legislatures in regard to said matters.</u>

50. Distribution of Legislative powers subject-wise between the Federal Legislature and a State or Provincial Legislature refers to those matters which are within the legislative power of the State. For the purpose of determining the legislative competence of a Legislature to consider such distribution of legislative powers as of greater consequence, than complete stripping of the legislative powers, as is provided in the Chapter containing the fundamental rights on the view that constitutional prohibitions regarding thereto, are mere legislative checks or that they render the law made in violation thereof "relatively void" or merely "unenforceable" appears to be a kind of casuistry for which there seems to be little justification. The doctrine of eclipse can be made applicable, although the term does not appear to be self explanatory only to a pre-constitutional law which is otherwise a good law but, of which on the enforcement of fundamental rights life breath has been taken out, It remains in a State of suspended animation and on the removal of the spell, as it were, it springs back into life, of its own motion without any further legislative effort. If the theory of subject-wise distribution of legislative powers as the only basis of legislative incompetence is accepted then there can hardly be any case of a law being void ab initio under a unitary Constitution.

<u>51. The East Pakistan Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 was enacted at a time when the fundamental right as incorporated in Right Nos.13 and 15 of 1962 Constitution of Pakistan were in full force and therefore the provisions incorporated in sections 4and 6 of the said Ordinance were void ab initio and as such could not be brought into life without fresh legislation, by mere repeal or abrogation of the Constitution which embodied the fundamental right.</u>

<u>52. Mr. Gafur, the learned Advocate for the opposite party has submitted that in spite of the decision of the Special Bench of the Dacca High Court, the Ordinance which was initially promulgated for a temporary period was being re-enacted from time to time and therefore it cannot be said that the law was really dead. The main question in his case is, whether on the 6th September, 1965 on which day the impugned auction sale was held, the unconstitutional provisions of the Ordinance could be deemed to have been brought into life on the Proclamation of Emergency suspending certain fundamental rights. The law was dead one in February, 1964 when the Ordinance was first enacted or in June, 1964 when the life of this Ordinance was sought to be extended, therefore whatever might have been the value of reenactment of the Ordinance after the proclamation of Emergency, there is no gainsaying that the relevant provisions of the Ordinance had no legal existence on the 6th September, because of their conflict with fundamental rights. Mr. Gafur has also submitted that the order which has been passed in pursuance of Ordinance No. 1 of 1964 should not be interfered with because this Ordinance was enacted in furtherance of a public policy and has been accepted to be so by the Government of Bangladesh and the learned Advocate has drawn my attention to a newspaper notice purported to have been issued by the Government of Bangladesh, in which it has been stated that the Ordinance has remained in force throughout the period from February, 1964 to the 31st March, 1969. This contention of the learned Advocate cannot be accepted. If this is a question of public policy I am not aware of any public policy, more sacred and more compulsive than upholding the constitutional guarantee in respect of fundamental rights, and the only public policy which may influence the decision of a Judge is that of deciding a case in accordance with the law of the country. The fact that the Government of Bangladesh has chosen to issue a public notice declaring that the Ordinance in question was in force throughout the period from February, 1964 till the end of March, 1969 in spite of the Special Bench's decision of the Dacca High Court striking down two sections of the said Ordinance, did not infuse any new life into those provisions which have been struck down. The only reasonable meaning which may be given to the said notice is that it has only the valid provisions of the Ordinance, i.e., the provisions other than those in section 4 and section 6 of the Ordinance which remained in force during the stated period.</u>

53. The learned Advocate has also submitted that, after all, the power that this Court exercises under section 115 C.P.C. is only discretionary and it should not be exercised in this case in view of the fact that some gross injustice appears to have been committed in getting the land measuring 2.20 acres sold for Tk. 70/- and odd only which is unreasonably low. This submission of the learned Advocate also is not tenable. There was patent irregular exercise of jurisdiction on a wrong view of law which is of some public importance. The impugned order therefore cannot be sustained and must be set aside. I am not, however, upholding the auction sale, which according to the learned Advocate, has been brought about by practicing fraud upon the Court. If the opposite party has got any case, he will be perfectly within his right to establish in the Court below by producing necessary evidence in this regard. Therefore there is no question of perpetuating any injustice by setting aside the main order.

54. The result therefore is that the Rule is made absolute and the order setting aside the auction sale in question is set aside and the case is sent back to the trial Court for hearing the application under Order 21, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure, on merits. The parties will be at liberty to produce necessary evidence in support of their respective cases. There shall be no order as to costs in this Rule.

End.
